entries.clause: Bolstad, chapter 8, Example 14 and the chapter's Main Points (pp. 147-155), with equations 8.3 and 8.5: for a binomial proportion, a beta(a, b) prior combined with y successes in n trials gives a beta posterior with parameters a' = a + y and b' = b + n - y; in words, the successes are added to a and the failures to b. Because the beta family is conjugate for binomial data, this posterior is found without integration. Equation 8.3 gives its mean, a' / (a' + b'), and equation 8.5 its variance, a'b' / ((a' + b')^2 (a' + b' + 1)). The printed values checked are from Table 8.2 (p. 152) and from chapter 16, Example 28.

entries.clause: Bolstad, chapter 10 (Positive uniform prior density, pp. 184-185; Example 17, pp. 187-190; Table 10.2): for n independent Poisson(mu) counts y_1, ..., y_n, the likelihood, as a function of mu, is shaped like a gamma density whose shape is one more than the total of the counts and whose rate is n. The positive uniform prior (g(mu) = 1 for every mu > 0) is improper, yet the posterior it gives is proper and has that same shape: gamma with shape (sum of y) + 1 and rate n. Under this prior, Example 17's eight weekly counts give gamma(27, 8).

entries.clause: Bolstad, chapter 11 (equations 11.5-11.6, p. 209; Example 20, pp. 210-213; Known Variance, p. 212): for n independent observations from a normal(mu, sigma^2) distribution whose variance sigma^2 is known, the sample mean has a normal distribution of mean mu and variance sigma^2 / n. With a normal(m, s^2) prior (or a flat prior), mu then has the posterior normal(m', (s')^2), updated as follows: a precision is one over a variance; the posterior's precision is the prior's precision plus the sample mean's precision, n / sigma^2; and m', the posterior mean, averages m and the sample mean, each weighted by its precision's share of the posterior precision.

entries.clause: Barber, sections 9.1.3-9.1.4 (equations 9.1.24-9.1.26 and 9.1.28-9.1.31): for a coin whose probability of heads is theta, a Beta(alpha, beta) prior with N_H heads and N_T tails observed gives the posterior Beta(alpha + N_H, beta + N_T); prior and posterior share the Beta form, so Beta priors are conjugate for binomial data. The posterior probability that theta is below 0.5 is then I_0.5(alpha + N_H, beta + N_T), I_x(a, b) denoting the regularised incomplete Beta function; with a flat prior (alpha = beta = 1), 2 heads and 8 tails give I_0.5(N_H + 1, N_T + 1) = 0.9673.

entries.clause: Barber, section 27.4.2 (equation 27.4.7, p. 547) and Algorithm 27.3, Metropolis-Hastings sampling (steps 4-10, p. 548): at step l a candidate x_cand is proposed from q~(x' | x_(l-1)), and the ratio a = q~(x_(l-1) | x_cand) p(x_cand) / (q~(x_cand | x_(l-1)) p(x_(l-1))) is formed. When a is 1 or more the candidate becomes x_l; otherwise u is drawn from the uniform distribution on [0, 1] and the candidate becomes x_l if u < a, while if not x_l stays equal to x_(l-1). This accepts with probability min(1, a), the acceptance function of equation 27.4.7, which is unchanged when p is replaced by an unnormalised p*.

entries.clause: Barber, section 12.2.2 (equations (12.2.5) to (12.2.7), pp. 267-268, and Example 12.2): for a coin whose probability of heads is theta, with a Beta(a, b) prior (chosen for its conjugacy with the binomial), the likelihood of the fair-coin model given data D of N_H heads and N_T tails is p(D | M_fair) = the integral over theta of p(theta) theta^N_H (1 - theta)^N_T, which equals B(N_H + a, N_T + b) / B(a, b), B being the Beta function. The fair coin's prior is Beta(50, 50); Example 12.2 applies this to 5 heads and 2 tails, and to 50 heads and 20 tails.

entries.clause: Barber, section 18.1.6, Prediction and model averaging, equation (18.1.45): when a prior is placed on the hyperparameters Gamma in addition to the weights w, the mean prediction at x averages f(x; w) over the joint posterior of w and Gamma given the data D: f-bar(x) = the double integral of f(x; w) p(w, Gamma | D) dw dGamma, which equals the integral over Gamma of [the integral of f(x; w) p(w | Gamma, D) dw] p(Gamma | D) dGamma. The inner integral is the predictor's mean at a fixed Gamma, so the outer integral weights each such mean by Gamma's posterior probability.

entries.title: Rank-normalization, folding, and localization: An improved R-hat for assessing convergence of MCMC
entries.derivation: Source notes require R-hat <1.01. Split first; average pooled ranks for ties; z=Phi^-1((r-3/8)/(S+1/4)); fold about pooled median; maximum of rank and folded R-hat; tail ESS minimum at 5% and 95%. ESS uses within and between chain variance; each chain's autocorrelation weighted by its variance s2_m (equation 10: with divisor-N autocovariances, acov_t N/(N-1)); Geyer's initial positive monotone paired sums, the first pair always kept (equations 12-13); and the average of the sums truncated at the usual odd lag and at the next even lag, bounded by S log10(S) (p. 8). Tail ESS shares bulk ESS's 400: Figure 5 (p. 13) marks 400 as the recommended level on its plot of bulk and tail ESS. The hand-computed tests are G6 algebra applying equations 1-4 and 10-13, not examples printed in the paper.
entries.clause: Vehtari et al. (2021), section 2, p. 4: the authors propose an R-hat computed on rank-normalized, folded draws (their section 4) and recommend using the sample only when it is below 1.01, with four or more chains as the default. Section 2, p. 5: they recommend requiring the rank-normalized effective sample size (ESS) to exceed 400. Section 3.2, p. 8: the authors' software bounds the ESS estimate above by S log10(S), for S draws.
entries.section: Section 2, pp. 4-5 (four chains, R-hat below 1.01, rank-normalized ESS above 400); 3.1-3.2, pp. 5-8 (split R-hat; ESS, equations 10-13, the next-even-lag average and the S log10(S) bound); 4.1-4.3, pp. 9-10; Figure 5 caption, p. 13 (400 on bulk and tail ESS)

entries.clause: DLMF 8.17.22-23: the regularised incomplete beta function I_x(a,b) equals x^a (1-x)^b / (a B(a,b)) times the continued fraction 1/(1+ d_1/(1+ d_2/(1+ ...))), with d_2m = m(b-m)x / ((a+2m-1)(a+2m)) and d_2m+1 = -(a+m)(a+b+m)x / ((a+2m)(a+2m+1)). The page says the fraction converges fast for x below (a+1)/(a+b+2); elsewhere I_(1-x)(b,a) is computed and the symmetry 8.17.4, I_x(a,b) = 1 - I_(1-x)(b,a), gives the value.
